question.text:
Consider a relation $R$ that is defined on the set $A = \left\{-2, 1, 5 \right\}.$ Given that $R$ is symmetric, enter the missing values in the adjacency matrix.

Note: If there is not enough information to determine a particular cell's value, then select the question mark $(\textrm{?}).$
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

We are given elements of the adjacency matrix in the following highlighted cells outside the diagonal:

$-2$ $1$ $5$
$-2$ $1$
$1$ $0$ $1$
$5$ $1$ $0$

As a result, the relation contains the pairs $(-2,5)$ and $(5,1).$ Since $R$ must be symmetric, we require

\[ (5,-2) \in R, \qquad (1,5) \in R. \]

So, the cells corresponding to these elements must all equal $1.$

$-2$ $1$ $5$
$-2$ $1$
$1$ $0$ $1$ $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}$
$5$ $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}1}$ $1$ $0$

Also, note the following:

  • The symmetric relation condition is equivalent to $(x,y)\notin R \Longrightarrow (y,x) \notin R.$ Therefore, $(1,-2)\notin R$ implies $(-2,1) \notin R.$

  • We do not have enough information to determine whether $(-2,-2)$ is an element of $R.$

Let's add this information to our table.

$-2$ $1$ $5$
$-2$ $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}?}$ $\bbox[3pt,Gainsboro]{\color{blue}0}$ $1$
$1$ $0$ $1$ ${\color{blue}1}$
$5$ ${\color{blue}1}$ $1$ $0$

question.text:
Consider a relation $R$ that is defined on the set $A = \{ 3, 6, 9 \}.$ Given that $R$ is antisymmetric, enter the missing values in the adjacency matrix.

Note: If there is not enough information to determine a particular cell's value, then select the question mark $(\textrm{?}).$
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

We are given elements of the adjacency matrix in the following highlighted cells outside the diagonal:

$3$ $6$ $9$
$3$ $1$ $0$
$6$ $1$ $0$
$9$ $1$ $1$

As a result, the relation contains the pairs $(6,3)$ and $(9,6).$ Since $R$ must be antisymmetric, we require

question.text:
Which of the following relations are antisymmetric?

  • $x \: R \: y$ if and only if $y=\dfrac1{x},$ defined on $\mathbb{R}^+$

  • $x \: S \: y$ if and only if $x \mid y,$ defined on $\mathbb{N}$

  • $x \: T \: y$ if and only if $x + 2y \geq 0,$ defined on $\mathbb{R}$
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In other words, if a pair $(x,y)$ belongs to a symmetric relation, then the pair $(y,x)$ should also be in the relation.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] In other words, only one of the pairs, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be in an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows pairs of the form $(x,x).$

With that in mind, let's examine our relations.

  • Relation $R$ is not antisymmetric. Notice that

    • $\left(2,\dfrac12\right) \in R$ since $\dfrac1{2} = \dfrac1{(2)},$ and

    • $\left(\dfrac12, 2\right) \in R$ since $2=\dfrac{1}{(1/2)}.$

  • Relation $S$ is antisymmetric. Indeed, if $(x,y) \in S$ and $(y,x) \in S,$ then $x = y.$ Notice that \[ x \mid y \quad \textrm{and} \quad y \mid x \qquad \Longrightarrow\qquad x = y \] for all $x,y \in \mathbb{N}.$

  • Relation $T$ is not antisymmetric. Notice that

    • $(2,1) \in T$ since $2 + 2(1) \geq 0,$ and

    • $(1,2) \in T$ since $1 + 2(2) \geq 0.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$S$ only."

example.title: Symmetric and Antisymmetric Over Infinite Sets

question.text: Which of the plots above represents a relation defined on the set $A=\{a,b,c\}$ that is both symmetric and antisymmetric?
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In terms of a plot, if a point $(x,y)$ belongs to the plot, then $(y,x),$ the point symmetric to $(x,y)$ over the diagonal line $y=x,$ should also be on the plot.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] So, only one of the points, either $(x,y)$ or $(y,x),$ can be on the plot of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows points on the diagonal line $y=x.$

With that in mind, let's draw the diagonal line $y=x$ and examine our plots.

  • Plot I represents neither a symmetric nor an antisymmetric relation. It's not symmetric since, for example, the point $(b,c)$ belongs to the plot while the point $(c,b)$ does not. And it's not antisymmetric since it contains the pairs $(a,b)$ and $(b,a).$

  • Plot II represents a symmetric relation since the plot is symmetric over the line $y = x.$

  • Plot III represents a relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric. Notice that it has no pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y.$ As a result, the propositions in both implications above are false. Hence, the implications themselves must be true.

Therefore, the correct answer is "III only."

question.text: Which of the above digraphs represents a relation, defined on the set $A = \{1,2,3\},$ that is both symmetric and antisymmetric?
question.explanation:
First, recall the following definitions:

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is symmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (y,x) \in R. \] In terms of a digraph, if we have an arrow $x \rightarrow y,$ then the arrow $y \rightarrow x$ must be in the digraph too.

  • A binary relation $R,$ defined on a set $A,$ is antisymmetric if for all $x,y \in A,$ we have \[ (x,y) \in R \quad\textrm{and}\quad (y,x) \in R \qquad\Longrightarrow\quad x=y. \] So, only one of the arrows, either $x \rightarrow y$ or $y \rightarrow x,$ can be in the digraph of an antisymmetric relation. Note that this condition allows loops.

With that in mind, let's examine our digraphs.

  • Digraph I represents a relation that is both symmetric and antisymmetric. Notice that it has no pairs of the form $(x,y)$ with $x \neq y.$ As a result, the propositions in both implications above are false. Hence, the implications themselves must be true.

  • Digraph II represents a symmetric relation since for every arrow $x \rightarrow y$ belonging to the graph, the corresponding inverse arrow $y \rightarrow x$ also belongs to the graph.

  • Digraph III represents an antisymmetric relation since for all possible $x$ and $y$ with $x \neq y,$ at most one of the arrows (either $x \rightarrow y$ or $y \rightarrow x,$ but not both) belongs to the digraph.

Therefore, the correct answer is "I only."
